code.title: Binary search: halve the window and count the looks
code.python:
# Time O(log n), space O(1): every look throws away half of the window.
def search(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    steps = 0
    while lo <= hi:                 # window [lo, hi] still has items
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2   # open the "dictionary" in the middle
        steps += 1
        if a[mid] == target:
            return mid, steps
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1            # target is after mid: drop left half
        else:
            hi = mid - 1            # target is before mid: drop right half
    return -1, steps                # window is empty: not present


a = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]
print("array: " + " ".join(map(str, a)))
for t in (23, 7):
    idx, steps = search(a, t)
    print(f"search {t} -> index {idx} in {steps} looks")

followUps:
Binary search needs random access because every step jumps straight to the middle item, and that jump must be cheap. In an array, a[mid] is one step, so about log2 n jumps cost O(log n) in total.

In a linked list you can only reach the middle by walking node by node. For 1,000,000 items the first jump alone walks 500,000 nodes, the next 250,000, and so on: about n steps in all. You still make only 20 comparisons, but the walking makes the search O(n), no better than a plain scan. That is why sorted linked data uses a skip list or a balanced tree instead.

The recursive version uses O(log n) extra space, because each call that halves the window waits on the call stack until the answer comes back.

The window halves on every call, so the deepest chain of calls is about log2 n. For 1,000,000 items that is roughly 20 stack frames, each holding lo, hi and mid. The loop version reuses the same three variables, so it needs O(1) space. Time is O(log n) for both.

The recursive call is the last thing the function does (a tail call), so some C++ compilers turn it into a loop, but Java and Python do not. In an interview, write the loop.

code.title: Midpoint overflow: (lo + hi) / 2 versus lo + (hi - lo) / 2
code.python:
# Python ints never overflow, so we imitate a 32-bit signed int by hand.
def to_int32(x):
    return (x + 2**31) % 2**32 - 2**31   # wrap into [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]


# Two valid 32-bit indexes whose sum does not fit in 32 bits.
lo, hi = 2000000000, 2100000000
print(f"lo = {lo}, hi = {hi}")

wrapped = to_int32(lo + hi)              # what a 32-bit language stores for lo + hi
bad = int(wrapped / 2)                   # the sum wrapped around to a negative number
safe = lo + (hi - lo) // 2               # hi - lo is small, so nothing can overflow
shift = (wrapped % 2**32) >> 1           # unsigned shift reads the wrapped bits as positive
signed = wrapped >> 1                    # signed shift keeps the wrong minus sign

print(f"(lo + hi) / 2       = {bad}")
print(f"lo + (hi - lo) / 2  = {safe}")
print(f"(lo + hi) >>> 1     = {shift}")
print(f"(lo + hi) >> 1      = {signed}")
# Each midpoint costs O(1) time and O(1) space; only the bad one is wrong.

followUps:
No, plain Python does not have this bug, because a Python int grows to as many digits as it needs and never wraps around.

Example: (2000000000 + 2100000000) // 2 gives 2050000000 in Python. In Java the same sum is stored in 32 bits, becomes -194967296, and the midpoint is -97483648.

Two cautions. First, fixed-width numbers do exist in Python libraries: a NumPy int32 array index or value can still overflow. Second, the habit lo + (hi - lo) // 2 is still worth keeping, because it is correct in every language and interviewers look for it.

>>> 1 works because it fills the top bit with 0, so the wrapped sum is read as a positive number; >> 1 copies the sign bit, so a wrapped (negative) sum stays negative.

The key fact: lo and hi are each below 231, so their true sum is below 232 and all of its bits still fit in 32 bits. Only the meaning of the top bit is wrong.

Tiny example with 8-bit numbers (max 127): 100 + 120 = 220, stored as 11011100, which reads as -36. Signed shift gives 11101110 = -18 (wrong). Unsigned shift gives 01101110 = 110, and 220 / 2 = 110 (right).

It only works for non-negative lo and hi. Both are O(1).

code.title: Lower bound with its loop invariant checked on every iteration

followUps:
You prove termination by showing that the window size is a whole number that gets strictly smaller on every pass and cannot go below zero.

For lower bound the size is hi - lo. Inside the loop lo < hi, and mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 rounds down, so lo ≤ mid < hi. Then either lo = mid + 1 (lo goes up by at least 1) or hi = mid (hi goes down by at least 1). Either way the size drops.

Example: lo = 4, hi = 5 gives mid = 4. The next state is (5, 5) or (4, 4): size 0, loop ends. A size that starts at n and at least halves each time ends after about log2 n passes.

The classic failure is lo = mid with a rounded-down mid: with lo = 4, hi = 5, mid = 4 and nothing changes, so it loops forever.

The right-hand half of the invariant breaks: “every index ≥ hi has a[i] ≥ x”.

When a[mid] ≥ x you have only learned something about index mid. Setting hi = mid keeps the statement true. Setting hi = mid - 1 also claims that a[mid - 1] ≥ x, which nobody checked.

Example: a = [1, 3, 5], x = 3, lo = 0, hi = 3. mid = 1 and a[1] = 3 ≥ 3, so hi becomes 0. Now the invariant says a[0] ≥ 3, but a[0] = 1. The loop ends with lo = 0 and returns index 0; the right answer is 1.

In short: in the half-open template hi is the first index already known to be ≥ x, so it must land on mid, not past it.

code.title: Two templates side by side: lo <= hi (exact match) and lo < hi (first true)

followUps:
With lo ≤ hi you test mid against both neighbours, return it if it is a peak, and otherwise step to the side that is higher.

  1. Treat positions outside the array as minus infinity.
  2. If the left neighbour is higher, a peak lies on the left: hi = mid - 1.
  3. Otherwise the right neighbour is higher: lo = mid + 1.
while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
  boolean upL = mid == 0 || a[mid-1] < a[mid];
  boolean upR = mid == n-1 || a[mid] > a[mid+1];
  if (upL && upR) return mid;
  if (!upL) hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid + 1;
}

For [1, 3, 7, 8, 6]: mid = 2 (7 < 8, go right), then mid = 3 (7 < 8 > 6), return 3. O(log n) time, O(1) space. It needs two comparisons and two edge checks per step, which is why the lo < hi form is usually preferred.

Starting with hi = n gives the search a way to answer “no such index”: the result n means every element is too small.

For “first index with a[i] ≥ x” there are n + 1 possible answers, 0 to n, not n. With a = [1, 3, 5] and x = 9 the correct answer is 3, the place where 9 would be inserted. If you start with hi = n - 1 = 2 the loop returns 2, and you need an extra check after the loop to notice that a[2] < 9.

It also buys you:

  • an empty array works with no special case (lo = hi = 0, loop never runs);
  • no out-of-range read, because mid < hi always, so a[n] is never touched;
  • simple counting: upperBound - lowerBound is the number of copies.

code.title: First and last occurrence of a target, and its count

followUps:
Count them as upperBound(R) - lowerBound(L): the first index with a value above R, minus the first index with a value at least L.

Everything from lowerBound(L) up to, but not including, upperBound(R) lies in [L, R], because the array is sorted.

Example: a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 8], range [2, 5]. lowerBound(2) = 1, upperBound(5) = 7, so the count is 7 - 1 = 6 (the values 2, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5).

int lo = lowerBound(a, L);   // first a[i] >= L
int hi = upperBound(a, R);   // first a[i] > R
return hi - lo;              // 0 if nothing is in range

Two binary searches: O(log n) time, O(1) space. L and R do not need to be present in the array.

Python has bisect.bisect_left and bisect.bisect_right; C++ has std::lower_bound, std::upper_bound and std::equal_range.

  • bisect_left(a, x) / lower_bound: first index with a value ≥ x.
  • bisect_right(a, x) / upper_bound: first index with a value > x.
  • equal_range: both at once, as a pair.

For a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3] and x = 2: left gives 1, right gives 4, so first = 1, last = 4 - 1 = 3, count = 3. Always check a[left] == x before trusting it, since both return an insert position when x is missing.

C++ returns iterators, so subtract a.begin() to get an index. Java's Arrays.binarySearch is not a substitute: with duplicates it may return any matching index. All are O(log n).

code.title: Search in a rotated sorted array (with duplicates handled)

followUps:
The rotation count is the index of the smallest element, and you can find it in O(log n) by comparing the middle with the last element.

  1. If a[mid] > a[hi], the drop is to the right of mid, so the minimum is in (mid, hi].
  2. Otherwise mid is in the low part, so the minimum is in [lo, mid].
int lo = 0, hi = n - 1;
while (lo < hi) {
  int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
  if (a[mid] > a[hi]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;
}
return lo;   // index of the minimum

For [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]: mid = 3 (7 > 2, lo = 4), mid = 5 (1 ≤ 2, hi = 5), mid = 4 (0 ≤ 1, hi = 4). Answer 4: the array was rotated 4 places. An unrotated array gives 0. O(log n) time, O(1) space, for distinct values.

Find the index p of the smallest element first; that splits the array into two normally sorted pieces, and you run an ordinary binary search on the piece that can hold the target.

  1. Find p by comparing a[mid] with a[hi] (go right if it is bigger).
  2. If a[p] ≤ target ≤ a[n-1], search [p, n-1]; otherwise search [0, p-1].
int p = minIndex(a);
if (a[p] <= target && target <= a[n-1])
  return binarySearch(a, p, n - 1, target);
return binarySearch(a, 0, p - 1, target);

For [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] and target 5: p = 4; 5 is not in [0, 2], so search indexes 0 to 3 and find it at 1. Two passes of O(log n) each, O(1) space. It is easier to get right than the one-pass version, at the cost of about twice the comparisons.

code.title: Find a peak in an unsorted array by always walking uphill
code.python:
# Time O(log n), space O(1). Needs neighbours to differ.
def find_peak(a):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2       # mid < hi, so mid + 1 is a valid index
        print(f"  lo={lo} hi={hi} mid={mid} a[mid]={a[mid]} a[mid+1]={a[mid + 1]}")
        if a[mid] < a[mid + 1]:
            lo = mid + 1                # uphill to the right: a peak is in (mid, hi]
        else:
            hi = mid                    # downhill: a peak is in [lo, mid]
    return lo                           # one candidate left: it is a peak


a = [1, 3, 7, 8, 6, 4, 9, 2]
print("array: " + " ".join(map(str, a)))
p = find_peak(a)
print(f"peak at index {p} with value {a[p]}")

followUps:
In a grid you binary search over the columns: look at the middle column, find its largest cell, and move towards whichever side neighbour is bigger.

  1. Take the middle column and scan it for its maximum, at row r.
  2. If that cell is at least as big as its left and right neighbours, it is a peak (it already beats the cells above and below).
  3. Otherwise move to the half that holds the bigger neighbour; a peak must exist there.

Example:

1  4  3
6  7  2
5  9  8

Middle column is (4, 7, 9); its maximum is 9, and its neighbours 5 and 8 are smaller, so 9 is a peak.

Each step costs one column scan of n rows and halves the m columns: O(n log m) time, O(1) space, against O(n m) for checking every cell.

No. Finding the largest value in an unsorted array needs a look at every element, so it takes at least n steps.

The reason is simple: if you skip even one position, the biggest value could be hiding there. For [1, 3, 7, 8, 6, 4, 9, 2] the peak search returns index 3 (value 8) after 3 comparisons, and it never reads the 9 at index 6.

A peak is a local property: you can confirm it by reading two neighbours, and the “walk uphill” rule guarantees one on the chosen side. The global maximum is not: nothing you see in one half tells you about the other half.

O(log n) for the maximum is possible only with extra structure, for example a sorted array (last element), a rotated sorted array, or a mountain array that rises and then falls once.

code.title: Binary search on the answer: Koko's minimum eating speed
code.python:
# Feasibility check: can Koko finish all piles in h hours at this speed? O(n)
def ok(piles, h, speed):
    hours = sum((p + speed - 1) // speed for p in piles)   # ceil(p / speed)
    return hours <= h


# Time O(n log(maxPile)), space O(1).
def min_speed(piles, h):
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)          # answer range is [1, max pile]
    while lo < hi:                  # find the first speed where ok is true
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if ok(piles, h, mid):
            hi = mid                # works: try something slower
        else:
            lo = mid + 1            # too slow: must go faster
    return lo


def show(piles, h):
    print("piles: " + " ".join(map(str, piles)) + f", hours: {h} -> minimum speed {min_speed(piles, h)}")


show([3, 6, 7, 11], 8)
show([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 5)
show([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 6)

followUps:
Start with a small guess and keep doubling it until the check passes; that doubled value becomes hi, and the previous one becomes lo.

  1. Set hi = 1.
  2. While ok(hi) is false, set hi = hi * 2.
  3. Binary search between hi / 2 and hi.
long hi = 1;
while (!ok(hi)) hi *= 2;
long lo = hi / 2;      // ok(lo) was false (or lo is 0)
// first true is in (lo, hi]

If the true answer is 37, the probes are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64: seven calls, then about five more to search 33 to 64. For an answer A that is about 2 log2 A calls to ok, so the cost depends on the answer, not on a huge guessed bound. Use a 64-bit type so the doubling cannot overflow.

When each check is very expensive, the goal changes from fast code to as few checks as possible, so you shrink the range first and stop as soon as the answer is precise enough.

  • Tighten the bounds with cheap knowledge (last month's result, a quick estimate). Going from a range of 1,000,000 to 1,000 saves 10 runs, or 100 minutes at 10 minutes each.
  • Stop early: if “within 5%” is enough, do not run the last few halvings.
  • Run in parallel: with 3 machines test 3 points at once and cut the range to a quarter per round, so 20 rounds become 10.
  • Cache results so no point is ever tested twice.
  • Handle noise: a load test can pass once and fail once. Repeat near the boundary, or the search can settle on the wrong side.

Total cost is (number of checks) × (cost of one check).

code.title: Aggressive Cows: greedy placement check inside a binary search
code.python:
# Greedy: put each cow in the first stall at least d away from the previous cow.
def placed(stalls, d):
    count, last = 1, stalls[0]          # first cow goes in the leftmost stall
    for s in stalls[1:]:
        if s - last >= d:
            count += 1
            last = s
    return count


# Time O(n log n) to sort + O(n log(range)) to search; space O(1) extra.
stalls = [1, 2, 8, 4, 9]
cows = 3
print("stalls: " + " ".join(map(str, stalls)) + f", cows: {cows}")
stalls.sort()                           # greedy needs left-to-right order
print("sorted: " + " ".join(map(str, stalls)))

lo, hi, best = 1, stalls[-1] - stalls[0], 0
while lo <= hi:                         # find the last distance that is feasible
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    c = placed(stalls, mid)
    print(f"  distance {mid}: greedy places {c} cows")
    if c >= cows:
        best = mid                      # works: try a bigger gap
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid - 1                    # fails: gap is too big
print(f"largest minimum distance = {best}")

followUps:
The stalls must be sorted because the greedy check walks from left to right and only compares each stall with the last cow it placed; that is only meaningful when positions are in increasing order.

In sorted order, the nearest cow to any new stall is always the previous one placed, so “gap to the last cow ≥ d” guarantees the gap to every earlier cow is ≥ d too.

Example: stalls [1, 2, 8, 4, 9], d = 3, 3 cows. Unsorted scan: place at 1, skip 2, place at 8, then 4 - 8 = -4 and 9 - 8 = 1 both fail: only 2 cows, so it wrongly reports “not possible”. Sorted [1, 2, 4, 8, 9]: place at 1, 4, 8: 3 cows, possible.

Sorting also gives the search range: the largest useful distance is last - first. Sorting costs O(n log n) once; each check is then O(n).

Feasibility is monotonic because a placement that keeps every pair of cows at least d apart also keeps them at least d - 1 apart, so if distance d works then every smaller distance works too.

Proof: suppose d is feasible. Take the placement that proves it. Every gap is ≥ d, and d > d - 1, so the very same placement shows d - 1 is feasible. Repeating the step gives d - 2, d - 3, and so on. Turned around: if d is not feasible, no larger distance is, because a placement for d + 1 would also be one for d.

So the answers look like true, true, true, false, false: one switch, which is exactly what binary search needs. For stalls [1, 2, 4, 8, 9] and 3 cows, distances 1, 2, 3 are feasible and 4 to 8 are not; the answer is the last true, 3.

code.title: Painter's Partition: search [max, sum] with 64-bit numbers
code.python:
# Greedy: how many painters are needed if nobody may paint more than limit?
def painters_needed(boards, limit):
    painters, load = 1, 0
    for b in boards:
        if load + b > limit:        # start a new painter
            painters += 1
            load = 0
        load += b
    return painters


# Time O(n log(sum)), space O(1). Python ints grow as needed, so no overflow here.
def min_time(boards, k):
    lo, hi = max(boards), sum(boards)    # range [max, sum]
    while lo < hi:                       # first limit that k painters can meet
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if painters_needed(boards, mid) <= k:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def show(boards, k):
    print("boards: " + " ".join(map(str, boards)) + f", painters: {k} -> minimum time {min_time(boards, k)}")


show([10, 20, 30, 40], 2)
show([2000000000, 1500000000, 1000000000], 2)   # sum is above 32-bit int range

followUps:
If the boards given to one painter no longer have to be next to each other, the simple greedy check stops working and the problem becomes NP-hard, so no fast exact method is known.

With contiguous sections, the check “fill a painter until the limit, then start the next” is provably best. Without that rule the check turns into bin packing: can these items fit into k bins of size L? Even k = 2 is the classic partition problem.

Example: boards [8, 7, 6, 5, 4], k = 2, total 30. Contiguous best is [8, 7] | [6, 5, 4] = 15. Here free choice also gives 15 (8 + 7 and 6 + 5 + 4), but greedy by size does worse: 8, 5, 4 = 17 against 7, 6 = 13.

In practice: for small n use bitmask DP, O(3n) or O(n 2n); for large n use a heuristic such as “largest item to the least loaded worker”, which is within 4/3 of the best.

The DP gives the same answer but is far slower: O(k n2) time and O(k n) space, against O(n log(sum)) time and O(1) space for binary search.

The DP is dp[j][i] = best result for the first i boards with j painters = the minimum over every split point p of max(dp[j-1][p], sum of boards p+1..i). Trying every p for every (j, i) costs k × n × n.

DPBinary search + greedy
n = 105, k = 101011 stepsabout 5 × 106
SpaceO(k n)O(1)
Needs a monotonic checknoyes

Choose the DP only when n is small (a few hundred) or the cost rule is not monotonic, for example when each painter has a different speed or set-up cost that breaks the greedy check.

code.title: Median of two sorted arrays by cutting the shorter one
code.python:
NEG, POS = -10**18, 10**18


# Time O(log(min(m, n))), space O(1).
def median(A, B):
    if len(A) > len(B):
        A, B = B, A                         # always cut the shorter array
    m, n = len(A), len(B)
    half = (m + n + 1) // 2
    lo, hi = 0, m
    while lo <= hi:
        i = lo + (hi - lo) // 2             # i items from A, j items from B
        j = half - i
        aL = NEG if i == 0 else A[i - 1]    # sentinels at the edges
        aR = POS if i == m else A[i]
        bL = NEG if j == 0 else B[j - 1]
        bR = POS if j == n else B[j]
        if aL > bR:
            hi = i - 1                      # A gave too many: move the cut left
        elif bL > aR:
            lo = i + 1                      # A gave too few: move the cut right
        else:
            left = max(aL, bL)
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1:
                return float(left)          # odd total: middle item
            return (left + min(aR, bR)) / 2 # even total: average of the two middles
    return -1.0


def show(A, B):
    print("A: " + " ".join(map(str, A)) + " | B: " + " ".join(map(str, B)) + f" -> median {median(A, B):.1f}")


show([1, 3, 8, 9, 15], [7, 11, 18, 19, 21, 25])
show([1, 2], [3, 4])

followUps:
Use the same cut idea, but make the left side hold exactly k elements instead of half of them; the answer is the largest element on the left side.

  1. Take i elements from A and j = k - i from B.
  2. i can only range over max(0, k - n) to min(k, m), so that j stays between 0 and n.
  3. The cut is right when A[i-1] ≤ B[j] and B[j-1] ≤ A[i].
int lo = Math.max(0, k - n), hi = Math.min(k, m);
while (lo <= hi) { int i = (lo + hi) / 2, j = k - i;
  if (i > 0 && j < n && A[i-1] > B[j]) hi = i - 1;
  else if (j > 0 && i < m && B[j-1] > A[i]) lo = i + 1;
  else return max(A[i-1], B[j-1]);  // skip a side that is empty
}

A = [1, 3, 8], B = [2, 7, 9], k = 4: i = 2, j = 2; 3 ≤ 9 and 7 ≤ 8, so the answer is max(3, 7) = 7. O(log(min(k, m))) time, O(1) space.

We search the shorter array so that the matching cut in the other array always lands inside it, and so that the number of steps depends on the smaller length.

The cut in B is fixed by the cut in A: j = half - i. If A is the shorter array (m ≤ n), then for every i from 0 to m, j stays between 0 and n. If A were longer, j could go negative.

Example: A has 5 elements, B has 2, so half = (5 + 2 + 1) / 2 = 4. Trying i = 5 gives j = 4 - 5 = -1, and B[j - 1] reads outside the array. Swapping so that the 2-element array is searched gives i in 0..2 and j in 2..4, all valid.

Cost is the second benefit: sizes 10 and 1,000,000 need about log2 10, roughly 4 steps, instead of 20.

code.title: A real use: bisecting commits to find the first bad one (like git bisect)
code.python:
tests = 0


# Pretend test run: commits before first_bad pass, the rest fail.
def is_bad(commit, first_bad):
    global tests
    tests += 1
    return commit >= first_bad


# Time O(log n) test runs, space O(1).
def bisect(n, first_bad):
    global tests
    lo, hi = 1, n                   # commit 1 is good, commit n is known bad
    tests = 0
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if is_bad(mid, first_bad):
            hi = mid                # bug already present: look earlier
        else:
            lo = mid + 1            # still good: bug came later
    return lo                       # first commit where the test fails


for n, first_bad in [(1000, 713), (1000000, 999999), (16, 1)]:
    found = bisect(n, first_bad)
    # A linear walk would need up to n test runs.
    print(f"{n} commits, bug introduced at {first_bad} -> found {found} after {tests} test runs")

followUps:
On 32 elements a straight scan can win because the processor handles a simple forward loop much better than a handful of unpredictable jumps.

  • Branch prediction: in a scan the test “not found yet” is true again and again, so the CPU guesses it right. In binary search each left/right choice is a coin flip; a wrong guess costs roughly 15 to 20 cycles, and there are about 5 of them.
  • Cache: 32 four-byte integers are 128 bytes, two cache lines, read in order.
  • SIMD: the compiler can compare 8 or 16 values in one instruction.

Rough numbers: 5 mispredicted branches cost about 75 to 100 cycles, while scanning 32 values with vector instructions takes a few cycles. That is why library sorts and B-tree nodes switch to a linear scan below a small size. Big-O hides constants; binary search wins clearly once n reaches the hundreds or thousands.

Keep a small index in memory that tells you which disk block to read, so that the search costs one or a few disk reads instead of one per halving.

A plain binary search over 1,000,000,000 records on disk touches about 30 different places, and each can be a separate disk read of milliseconds. Ways to cut that:

  • Sparse index: keep the first key of every block (say 4 KB) in RAM. Binary search that in memory, then read exactly one block and search inside it. This is how SSTables and Kafka index files work.
  • B+ tree: each node is one disk page holding hundreds of keys. With 500 keys per node, 4 levels cover 5004, about 6 × 1010 keys, so 4 reads at most, and the top levels stay cached.
  • Bloom filter in front to skip files that cannot contain the key.

The cost to count is disk reads: O(logB n), not comparisons.

code.title: Square root by bisection on doubles: epsilon loop versus fixed iterations

followUps:
About 50 iterations: each one halves the gap, and you need to shrink 109 down to 10-6, a factor of 1015.

After k halvings the gap is 109 / 2k. You need that to be at most 10-6, so 2k ≥ 1015, which gives k ≥ log2(1015) = 15 × 3.32 = 49.8. Round up to 50.

A handy rule: every 10 iterations gain about 3 decimal digits (210 is about 1000). 15 digits need 50 iterations.

General formula: iterations = ceil(log2((hi - lo) / eps)). In contests people simply run 100 iterations: it costs almost nothing and removes the need to think about it. A double holds only about 16 significant digits, so more than that cannot help.

Choose ternary search when you want the highest or lowest point of a function that goes one way and then the other (up then down, or down then up), and there is no yes/no test to binary search on.

It picks two points, m1 = lo + (hi - lo) / 3 and m2 = hi - (hi - lo) / 3. For a maximum: if f(m1) < f(m2) the peak cannot be left of m1, so lo = m1; otherwise hi = m2. Each round keeps two thirds of the range.

Example: f(x) = -(x - 3)2 on [0, 10]. m1 = 3.33, m2 = 6.67; f(m1) = -0.11 is bigger than f(m2) = -13.4, so hi = 6.67. The peak at 3 stays inside.

Cost: two evaluations per round and about log1.5 of the range rounds, so it is slower than binary search. If you can test the slope, for example f(mid) < f(mid + 1) on integers, binary search on that instead. Flat stretches break ternary search.
